ap-python.doThis: Run these parts at 1.5x and type every example into one notebook per part. Push it to a public apna-ai-ml repo the same night.
ap-python.why: You already write Python at work, so the lectures alone add little. What they can add is speed — and a public commit trail is proof a recruiter can actually open.
ap-python.harder: After each part, solve two small problems in Python from memory: comprehensions, generators, *args/**kwargs, a decorator.
ap-python.proof: Notebook committed · two problems solved without looking anything up

ap-data.doThis: Pick one public dataset (Kaggle is fine — never company data) and use it in every module instead of the toy examples.
ap-data.why: SQL and Pandas come up in most AI-engineer screens, and GROUP BY, joins and window functions are where candidates stall.
ap-data.harder: For every Pandas operation, write the SQL that does the same thing. Close SQL Part 2 with ten LeetCode SQL 50 problems.
ap-data.proof: One notebook analysing one dataset end to end · ten SQL problems logged

ap-math.doThis: One page of notes per module: the formula, and one line on where it shows up in ML. Nothing more.
ap-math.why: Interviews ask you to explain gradient descent, softmax and dot-product attention in words, not to derive proofs. Intuition is the bar.
ap-math.harder: Implement gradient descent for linear regression in plain NumPy — no sklearn — and plot the loss going down.
ap-math.proof: Three one-page sheets · a NumPy gradient-descent notebook

ap-ml.doThis: For every algorithm, fit it with sklearn, then write the short version yourself — module 29 shows how. Treat CreditWise and SmartCart as portfolio projects, not exercises.
ap-ml.why: Bias–variance, overfitting and precision-versus-recall are standard ML-round questions, and the two minor projects are your first AI lines on a resume.
ap-ml.harder: Give each minor project a README: problem, data, metric, result, what you would do next. Serve one behind a FastAPI endpoint.
ap-ml.proof: Two project repos with READMEs · one model behind an endpoint

ap-tools.doThis: Clear this in one sitting — you use Git every day. Put the saved time into the next ML module.
ap-tools.why: This is review for you. The only gaps worth closing are rebase, cherry-pick and resolving conflicts without fear.
ap-tools.harder: Write a GitHub profile README that links your course repos. It is the first thing a recruiter clicks.

ap-dl.doThis: Write the training loop yourself every time — forward, loss, backward, step. Never run the course cell as-is.
ap-dl.why: This is the largest block of Course 1 and the base for transformers in Course 2. Interview depth here is backprop, overfitting and choosing an architecture.
ap-dl.harder: For the Text Summarizer, compare two approaches and report ROUGE for both. A number you measured beats an adjective.
ap-dl.proof: Your own training-loop notebook · Text Summarizer repo with a metric

ap-apps.doThis: Build every example as an API, not a notebook. Start from your Flask background, then rewrite one in FastAPI.
ap-apps.why: AI-engineer roles hire for shipping LLM features behind an API — structured output, retries, cost and latency. This is the most job-shaped module in Course 1.
ap-apps.harder: Log token count and latency for every call, and add a retry with backoff. Mention both in the README.
ap-apps.proof: One deployed LLM endpoint with a README

ap-projects.doThis: Finish all four, then polish one — the AI Resume ATS — into your flagship: deployed, README with screenshots, a two-minute demo video.
ap-projects.why: One shipped project you can explain carries more weight in an interview than a list of courses, and the ATS project is the closest to AI-engineer work.
ap-projects.harder: Write a five-minute explanation for each: problem, design, tradeoffs, what broke, what you would change. Say it out loud once.
ap-projects.proof: Four repos · one deployed flagship · a written walkthrough for each

fm-nlp.doThis: Implement tokenisation, TF-IDF and cosine similarity by hand once, then switch to the libraries.
fm-nlp.why: Similarity search is the base of every RAG system later in this course. Doing it by hand once makes the libraries legible.
fm-nlp.harder: Build a tiny search over your own notes with TF-IDF, then swap in embeddings and compare results on the same ten queries.
fm-nlp.proof: A notebook comparing TF-IDF and embedding search side by side

fm-transformers.doThis: Read the actual paper alongside the videos, and build the Nano LLM yourself — every line typed.
fm-transformers.why: "Explain self-attention" and "why multi-head" are among the most common AI-engineer theory questions. Having built it is what makes the answer fluent.
fm-transformers.harder: Draw Q/K/V attention on paper from memory, then explain it out loud in two minutes.
fm-transformers.proof: A Nano LLM repo that trains and generates · a one-page attention sheet

fm-prompt.doThis: Keep every prompt in a versioned file next to the input and the output it produced.
fm-prompt.why: Prompting is judged as engineering now — reproducible, evaluated, versioned. That is the gap between a demo and a product.
fm-prompt.harder: Write a ten-case evaluation set for one prompt and score two versions of it.
fm-prompt.proof: A prompts folder with versions · an eval score comparing two of them

fm-rag.doThis: Build RAG over a real document set — the public 3GPP specs from your own domain are ideal — and measure retrieval, not just answers.
fm-rag.why: RAG is a staple of AI system-design rounds, and interviewers push on chunking, retrieval quality and hallucination — exactly where demos stay vague.
fm-rag.harder: Try three chunk sizes and report recall@5 for each. Add a reranker and show the difference.
fm-rag.proof: A RAG repo with a results table · faithfulness checked on 20 questions

fm-langchain.doThis: Build one small pipeline twice — once with LangChain, once with direct API calls — and note what each costs you.
fm-langchain.why: Teams want someone who can use a framework and also knows when not to. Having done both is the honest answer.
fm-langchain.harder: Write LCEL chains with structured output and a fallback when parsing fails.
fm-langchain.proof: Two implementations of one pipeline · a short comparison in the README

fm-agents.doThis: Build one agent that does real work: read a log file, find the errors, write a summary. Tools first, then memory, then multiple agents.
fm-agents.why: Agents and MCP are where AI-engineer work is moving. A working agent with clear tool boundaries is a strong portfolio piece — and log triage is your daily job.
fm-agents.harder: Add guardrails — a step limit, tool-input validation, a cost cap — and log every tool call.
fm-agents.proof: An agent repo with a demo run and its tool-call log

cs-c.doThis: Write every program from a blank file, compile with -Wall -Wextra, and run it under valgrind.
cs-c.why: C is your working language at Parallel Wireless, and pointer and memory questions are where systems interviews start.
cs-c.harder: Implement your own strlen, memcpy and a dynamic array that grows.
cs-c.proof: Programs in a repo · valgrind clean

cs-cpp.doThis: Move your DSA solutions to C++ and the STL now — that is where fluency comes from.
cs-cpp.why: STL fluency saves minutes in every timed round, and the rule of three/five and virtual dispatch are standard C++ questions.
cs-cpp.harder: Implement a minimal unique_ptr and a vector with move semantics.
cs-cpp.proof: An STL cheat sheet written from memory · both implementations

cs-lb.doThis: Three to five problems a day, smallest first. Write the approach in one line before you write code.
cs-lb.why: Logic building is the reflex DSA rounds test: turning a problem into steps, fast.
cs-lb.harder: Time every problem. Anything over 20 minutes goes on the Sunday re-solve list.
cs-lb.proof: Problems logged with time and pattern

cs-dsa.doThis: Log every problem in the DSA tab with its pattern, and re-solve one older problem cold each week.
cs-dsa.why: DSA is the highest-weight item in SDE loops at Amazon, Google and Microsoft, and recognising the pattern transfers further than raw problem count.
cs-dsa.harder: Explain each solution out loud as if to an interviewer: brute force, then optimised, then complexity.
cs-dsa.proof: Every pattern with at least three clean solves

cs-lsp.doThis: Write each system-call program yourself and trace it with strace.
cs-lsp.why: You work on telecom systems. Processes, threads, IPC and sockets set you apart from AI candidates who only know Python.
cs-lsp.harder: Build a multi-threaded TCP server that handles concurrent clients and shuts down cleanly.
cs-lsp.proof: A TCP server repo · strace notes

weekday.label: Wake up · water · no phone
weekday.note: A glass of water before anything else. The first ten minutes decide whether the day is yours or your feed’s.

weekday.label: Run or home workout
weekday.note: Outdoors when you can — it is also your daylight. After a short night, go easy rather than skip.

weekday.label: Shower · skin care (AM)
weekday.note: Cleanse, moisturise, sunscreen. Tied to the shower so it never needs remembering.

weekday.label: Breakfast — protein first
weekday.note: Eggs, paneer, dal, curd or sprouts before anything sweet. Morning items your doctor directed go here.

weekday.label: Recall yesterday’s notes · get ready
weekday.note: Twenty minutes: write what you remember from yesterday’s module, then check. Recall beats re-watching.

weekday.label: Office · commute both ways
weekday.note: The job comes first — deliver it well, the resume lines come from here. Spare time: watching and reading only.

weekday.label: Home · change · light snack
weekday.note: Fruit, roasted chana, buttermilk or nuts — not biscuits and sweet chai. This is where the evening sugar habit starts.

weekday.label: Block 1 — Course
weekday.note: Apna College first, Five Minute Engineering second. Code along — if you did not type it, you did not learn it.

weekday.label: Evening run
weekday.note: Protected. Fitness and recovery, not slack to raid when the day runs late.

weekday.label: Shower · skin + hair care (PM)
weekday.note: Night skin routine, and your hair-care routine exactly as directed.

weekday.label: Dinner — light, then the kitchen closes
weekday.note: Protein and vegetables, a smaller portion of rice or roti. Nothing to eat during the night block.

weekday.label: Block 2 — DSA + deep work
weekday.note: DSA first while you are sharpest, then build. Phone in another room.

weekday.label: Sleep
weekday.note: Screens off. Six hours is the floor, not the goal — the weekend pays it back.

saturday.label: Wake slow · water
saturday.note: Sleep in — five short nights are behind you. Still no phone for the first ten minutes.

saturday.label: Long easy run
saturday.note: Slower and longer than a weekday, at a pace where you could still talk. This builds the aerobic base.

saturday.label: Shower · skin care (AM)
saturday.note: Sunscreen matters more today — you will be on the bike later.

saturday.label: Breakfast — protein first
saturday.note: A proper meal before the long block. Morning items your doctor directed go here.

saturday.label: Deep block — the week’s hardest item
saturday.note: Three uninterrupted hours, the longest block of your week. Spend it on whatever needs the most focus.

saturday.label: Lunch · rest
saturday.note: Eat, walk ten minutes, lie down for twenty if you need it.

saturday.label: DSA — problems + one re-solve
saturday.note: Re-solve one problem from earlier in the week, cold. Retention is the metric.

saturday.label: Ride — Classic 350 to the hills
saturday.note: Small happiness, fully earned. Full gear, fuel before the ghat, down before it is fully dark. Stops: tender coconut, chaas, unsweetened chai.

saturday.label: Dinner
saturday.note: Eating out is fine: tandoor or grilled over fried, no dessert, no cold drinks.

saturday.label: Shower · skin + hair care (PM)
saturday.note: Wash off the road. Night routine, hair care exactly as directed.

saturday.label: Light block — revise the week
saturday.note: Recall-first revision of the week’s modules. Watching and reading only — you have ridden for four hours.

saturday.label: Free time
saturday.note: Guilt-free. A film, family, friends — the week was hard and this hour is yours.

saturday.label: Sleep
saturday.note: A full night. This is where the week’s short sleep gets paid back.

sunday.label: Wake slow · water
sunday.note: Another full night behind you. Water first, phone later.

sunday.label: Walk or mobility — recovery
sunday.note: Legs rest today. A brisk walk or twenty minutes of stretching keeps the habit without the load.

sunday.label: Breakfast — protein first
sunday.note: Morning items your doctor directed go here.

sunday.label: Deep block — clear the carry-over
sunday.note: Anything still open from the week goes first, so Monday starts clean.

sunday.label: Lunch · rest
sunday.note: Home food if you can. Cook extra for Monday.

sunday.label: Weekly timed DSA set
sunday.note: Three problems under time, no hints. Log the solve times — that is the number interviews measure.

sunday.label: Ride — short trip, back early
sunday.note: Back by 19:30. Sunday night resets the week; it should not be spent recovering from the ride.

sunday.label: Dinner
sunday.note: Light and early. Kitchen closes after this.

sunday.label: Weekly review · plan the week
sunday.note: Analytics → weekly review. Name one thing that slipped and the one change that fixes it.

sunday.label: Prep Monday — bag, clothes, office snacks
sunday.note: Pack nuts, fruit or chana for the office so the 4 pm craving already has an answer.

sunday.label: Skin + hair care (PM)
sunday.note: Night routine, hair care exactly as directed.

sunday.label: Light block — preview Monday’s module
sunday.note: Skim the first module of the week so Monday’s block starts warm.

sunday.label: Sleep — Monday starts at wake-up
sunday.note: Earlier tonight so Monday morning is not a fight.

healthFocus.label: Weight loss
healthFocus.track: Weekly weigh-in — same morning, same scale, before breakfast.
healthFocus.evidence: Weight loss comes from a sustained calorie deficit. Protein and fibre help with fullness, and short sleep tends to push appetite up.
do: Protein at every meal — eggs, paneer, dal, curd, chicken or fish.
Half the plate vegetables before the rice or roti.
Weigh in once a week, not every day.
avoid: Eating during the night block — it is the easiest 300 calories of the day.
Liquid calories: juice, sweet lassi, cold drinks, sugary chai.
Treating a good workout as a reason to eat freely.

healthFocus.label: Low sugar
healthFocus.track: Tick "No added sugar" on Today, every day you manage it.
healthFocus.evidence: Added sugar is energy with almost no fullness, and cutting sugary drinks is one of the most consistent findings in diet research.
do: Chai and coffee without sugar — or step down half a spoon a week.
Read the label on biscuits, granola and "healthy" bars.
avoid: Office celebration sweets — one piece, not three.
Cold drinks, at the office or on a ride. Tender coconut or chaas instead.

healthFocus.label: Triglycerides
healthFocus.track: Log each lipid panel in Labs, exactly as the report prints it.
healthFocus.evidence: Triglycerides respond strongly to lifestyle: less added sugar, fewer refined carbohydrates, little or no alcohol, and regular aerobic exercise are the standard first steps. Whether anything more is needed is your doctor’s call.
do: Keep both daily runs — aerobic exercise is the main lever.
Swap white rice and maida for whole grains where you can.
Fish or other omega-3-rich foods a couple of times a week, if you eat them.
avoid: Fried snacks and maida — samosa, vada pav, cream biscuits.
A big plate of rice late at night.

healthFocus.label: HDL (good cholesterol)
healthFocus.track: Log HDL with each lipid panel in Labs.
healthFocus.evidence: Regular aerobic exercise, losing excess weight, not smoking, and replacing trans fats with unsaturated fats are all associated with better HDL.
do: Aerobic exercise most days — your runs count.
Unsaturated fats: nuts, seeds, groundnut or mustard oil in normal amounts.
Keep the weight trend moving down.
avoid: Trans fats: vanaspati, reused frying oil, bakery puffs.
Sitting for hours — stand up once an hour at the office.

healthFocus.label: Vitamin B12
healthFocus.track: Tick your doctor-directed item on Today; log each level in Labs.
healthFocus.evidence: B12 comes mainly from animal foods — dairy, eggs, fish and meat — so a mostly vegetarian diet makes low levels more likely. Correcting it is your doctor’s plan, and retests show whether it is working.
do: Take exactly what your doctor directed, at the same time every day.
Dairy and eggs daily, if you eat them.
Retest when your doctor says, and log the result here.
avoid: Skipping doses on busy days — consistency is the whole point.
Changing the dose on your own.
Writing off tiredness as "just the schedule" — tell your doctor.

healthFocus.label: Vitamin D
healthFocus.track: Tick your doctor-directed item on Today; log each level in Labs.
healthFocus.evidence: The body makes vitamin D from sunlight on the skin, and an indoor office day provides very little. Supplements are taken as your doctor directs, often with a meal.
do: Take exactly what your doctor directed — ask whether it should go with a meal.
Run outdoors in the morning rather than on a treadmill.
Retest when your doctor says, and log the result here.
avoid: Taking extra on your own — vitamin D builds up in the body.
Spending every daylight hour indoors — step out for ten minutes at lunch.
